analysis.one_liner: Strengthens civil rights and permitting rules so communities of color and low-income areas get protection from pollution.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 15 senators from one party, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the Civil Rights Act so that federally funded programs that harm people based on race or national origin — even without intent — could be challenged in court, with attorneys' fees available. It would have required air and water pollution permits to account for the total, combined pollution a community already suffers, allowed permits to be denied to repeat violators, and created grant programs for parks, transit to trails, and research on safer chemicals. It was introduced in March 2023 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no further action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities that sit near polluting facilities would gain new legal tools and stronger permit protections. Urban neighborhoods with poor park access would gain grant funding, as would users of cosmetics and menstrual products through new ingredient labeling.

how_it_helps.text: Amends Title VI of the Civil Rights Act to bar federally funded programs that have a discriminatory effect based on race, color, or national origin, and gives aggrieved persons the right to sue, with attorney's and expert fees recoverable.

Requires air and water pollution permits to be evaluated against the cumulative pollution a community already faces, and allows permits to be denied if the permitting authority cannot find a reasonable certainty of no harm to public health.
Allows permitting authorities to deny permits to 'persistent violators' of the Clean Air Act, or to require them to submit and carry out community-reviewed compliance plans.

Directs federal agencies to prepare community impact reports and hold extended public comment periods for federal actions affecting environmental justice communities, and to consider alternatives proposed by the affected community itself.

Creates grant programs for park access in underserved urban areas, a transit-to-trails program authorized at $10 million per year, and research on safer alternatives to toxic chemicals in cosmetics, toys, and baby products.

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that emit pollution — the applicants for air and water permits — would bear the cost of cumulative-impact analyses, added controls, and possible permit denials. Manufacturers of cosmetics and menstrual products would face new labeling requirements. Some of these costs could be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Polluting facilities and consumer product makers

drawbacks.text: Requiring permit applicants to demonstrate a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' based on all pollution in a community, not just their own emissions, could add significant time and cost to permitting and could block some projects outright, including infrastructure projects that themselves provide public benefits.
The new private right of action under the Civil Rights Act, with fee-shifting, would expose federally funded entities to more litigation, including suits whose merits a court would have to sort out.

The park and transit grant programs generally require recipients to match the federal amount dollar-for-dollar, which can be a barrier for the poorest communities, though the Secretary may waive it in defined cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living in communities that bear a disproportionate share of pollution, the bill offered concrete protections: a court remedy, permit decisions that account for total community exposure, and money for parks and transit. The main costs — slower and costlier permitting and litigation risk — fall on permit applicants and polluting facilities, and some could reach consumers through prices. The one design weakness visible in the text is the 100% matching requirement for grants, which the Secretary could waive but which could still deter the neediest applicants.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a markup or vote on it, so the full Senate never got the chance to vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill in the Senate on March 22, 2023, joined by 13 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The full action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the referral was the last step the bill ever took in the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that emit pollution into fenceline communities — including sources that would have faced cumulative-impact permit tests, persistent-violator permit denials, and private lawsuits — avoid all of those requirements because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluting facilities that avoided new permit tests and lawsuits

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Environmental Justice For All Act in the Senate.

for.name: Cory Booker, Ed Markey, Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, and 10 other senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a one-party bloc of 15 supporters; none of them moved the bill past committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by a Democrat in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; the action history shows no floor scheduling at any point in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an independent, no Republican signed on in the record, and the bill never reached a vote where members would have had to take a position.

industries.industry: Pollution-emitting facilities (refineries, chemical plants, manufacturers with air and water permits)
industries.note: The bill would have required permit decisions to account for a community's total pollution burden, allowed permit denials for repeat violators, and opened facilities' federally funded activities to civil-rights lawsuits. Its interest in avoiding those tests runs directly against the health of the residents who live next to the emissions.
New ingredient-labeling requirements and safer-alternatives research would add compliance costs, though the same rules give consumers information about what is in the products they use daily.

industries.industry: Local governments, park districts, and transit agencies
industries.note: The bill would have created grant programs for park acquisition and transit-to-trails service, funded at the federal level with matching local contributions.
The bill includes just-transition assistance and economic revitalization programs aimed at communities and workers whose local economies depend on fossil fuel industries.
